November 14, 2022 
 
 
The Honorable Martin J. Walsh 
U.S. Department of Labor 
200 Constitution Avenue N.W. 
Washington, D.C. 20210 
 
RE: (RIN 1205-AC01) Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act Title I Non-Core Programs Effectiveness in 
Serving Employers Performance Indicator 
 
Dear Secretary Walsh, 
 
On behalf of Goodwill Industries International (GII), and our network of local Goodwill® organizations, thank you 
for the opportunity to respond to this Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) on the Workforce Innovation and 
Opportunity Act (WIOA) non-core programs performance indicator of effectiveness in serving employers. 
Goodwill works to enhance the dignity and quality of life of individuals and families by strengthening 
communities, eliminating barriers to employment, and helping people in need reach their full potential through 
learning and the power of work. 
At a time when millions of available jobs are going unfilled, Goodwill is helping to build employment pipelines of 
qualified workers that are equipped with the in-demand skills that employers need. Local Goodwill organizations 
provide career navigation, skills training, job placement, and other community-based services, such as English-
language training, financial education, industry-recognized credentials, résumé preparation, and access to 
reliable transportation and childcare. In 2021, Goodwill provided services to nearly 2 million people and helped 
more than 123,000 individuals secure new jobs and career advancement opportunities. In fact, one out of every 
624 U.S. hires last year was placed by Goodwill.   
Local Goodwill organizations also serve a vital role in the workforce system as operators of one-stop job centers 
and contributing partners in their workforce areas as providers of career services, job training, and holistic 
supports. More than 13,000 individuals were referred to Goodwill services through the workforce system last 
year. Public investments in WIOA programs and other federal resources help local Goodwills deliver high-quality 
employment and training to job seekers and career advancers in communities across the country.  
Goodwill also seeks to advance policy solutions that will strengthen the workforce system and improve 
employment outcomes for those facing barriers to opportunity, including people involved in the justice system, 
opportunity youth, older workers, people with disabilities, and veterans and military families. These comments 
are assimilated from the best lessons from the field, effective strategies, and insights of Goodwill team members 
and the people they serve. 
Serving People Impacted by the Justice System 
The U.S. Department of Justice estimates that more than 650,000 people are released from prison every year. 
The overwhelming majority of incarcerated people will return to their communities at some point, and many will 
confront significant challenges when reentering society. Goodwill leads the way in creating employment 

opportunities for justice-involved people. In 2021, local Goodwill organizations served more than 46,000 
individuals with a criminal background, including those reintegrating back into society. Since 2016, GII has 
engaged with 22 local Goodwill organizations to utilize $22 million in federal funding through six reentry grants 
that will serve more than 2,300 justice-involved individuals. Goodwill's evidence-based reentry services offer 
participants opportunities to engage in learning, skills development, work experience, and holistic reintegration 
services. 
The Department proposes through this NPRM to define the WIOA core indicator of performance for 
effectiveness in serving employers as “the percentage of participants with wage records who exited a program 
and were employed by the same employer in the second and fourth quarters after exit.” As specified by WIOA, 
the proposed measure would directly apply to four “non-core” programs authorized by WIOA title I. As noted in 
the NPRM, other WIOA non-core programs, including the Reentry Employment Opportunities (REO) grant 
program, are required under the guidance issued by the Department in Training and Employment Guidance 
Letter (TEGL) 14-18 to report on effectiveness in serving employers as a measure of retention with the same 
employer. Though the REO grant program is not directly addressed in this rulemaking, the NPRM indicates that 
the proposed definition of effectiveness in serving employers performance indicator would be applied to certain 
other non-core programs specified in TEGL 14-18, which includes REO.  
Given the guidance set forth in TEGL 14-18 and the Department’s stated intentions to apply the proposed 
definition to the REO program, it is incumbent upon the Department to provide grantees with clear guidance on 
the implications of the proposed definition on REO program performance accountability policies and practices 
going forward. Moreover, we believe that grantees and other stakeholders should be provided with further 
opportunities to address concerns, offer feedback, present questions, and share the insights of community-
based reentry service providers.  
The Department asserts in the NPRM that the approach of measuring effectiveness in serving employers 
through retention with the same employer was determined, following a state pilot program that examined three 
possible measures, to be the least burdensome of the options considered, and one that offers an established 
method of collecting the employment information of participants through the use of wage records. However, 
TEGL 14-18 advises REO grant recipients to collect and report “supplemental wage information,” such as 
paystubs or other forms of employment documentation, where wage records for participants are unavailable. In 
practice, this requires a significant commitment of time and effort by Goodwill reentry program staff to do 
follow up with participants in order to collect the information needed to establish employment outcomes.  
In addition, Goodwill reentry programs are reluctant to use employers as a source for supplemental wage 
information out of concerns that disclosure of a criminal background could jeopardize the participant’s 
employment prospects. While Goodwill has developed strong partnerships with fair-chance employers to 
facilitate job placements for justice-involved individuals, program participants are encouraged to take ownership 
over their career and life decisions and to pursue employment opportunities that are best suited to their skills, 
abilities, and goals. The Department should work with REO grant recipients and other workforce system 
stakeholders to ensure that reentry programs are able to access wage record data to more efficiently facilitate 
the collection and reporting of the employment outcomes of participants.  
We agree with the Department’s goal of promoting systems alignment through consistency and common 
language in performance across federal workforce programs. However, we believe that performance 
accountability for non-core employment and training programs should reflect the unique needs and 
circumstances of the distinct populations of job seekers and career advancers served by those programs. The 
Department also acknowledges in the NPRM that retention with the same employer as a measure of 
performance could result in unintended consequences, specifically noting that this approach would be at odds 
with those participants who might choose to leave their employer to pursue a position with better 

compensation. Justice-involved individuals who are reentering the workforce after a period of incarceration 
often need to build work experience in order to advance into career opportunities that can offer them family-
sustaining wages and benefits. While gaining job experience is an important first step toward a rewarding career 
for justice-involved workers, it is not in their best interests to continue with the same employer at the expense 
of achieving greater financial stability and opportunities for advancement. Effective reentry programs empower 
justice-involved individuals to overcome their barriers to employment so they can support themselves and their 
families and contribute to their communities. This should be recognized as a successful outcome for the 
workforce system.   
The Department should consider other outcomes for measuring effectiveness in serving employers that 
demonstrate a direct benefit to employers that are willing to hire justice-involved individuals, such as 
participation in the federal bonding program or by identifying those employers who take advantage of the Work 
Opportunity Tax Credit. We urge the Department to engage with the community of REO grantees to consider 
meaningful measures of program performance that will ensure that justice-involved Individuals have a fair 
chance for employment and a second chance for success. 
Recommendations: 
• 
Provide REO grantees with clear guidance on the implications of the proposed definition for 
program performance accountability policies and practices.  
• 
Make certain that grantees and other stakeholders have the opportunity to address concerns and 
offer feedback on the proposed definition and related rulemaking. 
• 
Ensure that grantees are able to access wage record data for the collection and reporting of the 
employment outcomes of participants. 
• 
Consider outcomes for effectiveness in serving employers that demonstrate a benefit to fair-chance 
employers, such as the federal bonding program or Work Opportunity Tax Credit. 
• 
Identify meaningful measures of program performance that will help ensure that justice-involved 
Individuals have a fair chance for employment and a second chance for success. 
Providing Employment Opportunities for Older Workers 
Local Goodwill organizations are dedicated to providing holistic employment and supportive services to older 
workers. The COVID-19 pandemic placed enormous hardships on older Americans who faced barriers to safely 
accessing training, community service, and job opportunities. Despite these challenges, older workers continue 
to serve a vital role in our workforce, and bring with them the knowledge, dedication, judgement, and insights 
gained through years of work and life experiences. 
Goodwill provided services to over 182,000 individuals aged 55 and older in 2021. Since October 2006, GII has 
been a national grantee for Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP), which is funded by the 
U.S. Department of Labor Employment and Training Administration. Participants must be unemployed, 55 years 
of age or older, have incomes no more than 125 percent of the federal poverty level and have a training need. 
Goodwill helps these older adults connect to employment and service opportunities, and to critical training (e.g., 
digital literacy) needed to meet the needs of today’s labor market. Local Goodwill organizations also offer older 
workers supportive services and job placement assistance. SCSEP is a key component in our nation’s workforce 
development system that is helping to address the employment challenges of older Americans, as well as the 
workforce needs of employers.  
In 2018, the Department issued a Final Rule adopting the Interim Final Rule (IFR) that revised performance 
accountability regulations for SCSEP that reflect changes in the Older Americans Act Reauthorization Act of 
2016. Although SCSEP includes performance indicators that are similar to the WIOA measure of effectiveness in 

serving employers, SCSEP differs in that it also measures the effectiveness in serving participants and host 
agencies as well. The IFR added a definition for the indicators of effectiveness in serving employers, host 
agencies, and participants as “the combined results of customer assessments of the services received by each of 
these three customer groups. 
The Final Rule states that the Department will continue surveying employers, host agencies, and participants for 
the purposes of assessing the effectiveness of services as “an interim measure at least until the WIOA pilot is 
complete and a WIOA measure is defined in final form.” However, it also correctly notes that the pilot approach 
to measuring effectiveness of serving employers is not applicable to SCSEP's other two customer groups. 
The IFR further states that the Department may revise the SCSEP definition once the definition of the 
corresponding WIOA performance measure is finalized. While SCSEP is not authorized by WIOA and not directly 
subject to this rulemaking, it was among the DOL-administered workforce programs included in TEGL 14-18 on 
aligning performance accountability reporting, definitions, and policies. The Department should make clear its 
intentions, if any, to engage in further rulemaking to change the definition of the performance indicator of 
effectiveness in serving employers as it applies to SCSEP. It is imperative that SCSEP grantees and stakeholders 
be afforded the opportunity to provide feedback and share concerns about any proposed changes in 
performance accountability policies and practices.   
In addition to the limitations on the collection and reporting of employment-based outcomes data experienced 
by Goodwill reentry programs, assessing employer satisfaction as a measure of retention with the same 
employer for SCSEP would also fail to account for the unique needs and employment patterns of the population 
served by the program. Health concerns, caregiving obligations, preferences for part-time or temporary 
employment, or other life circumstances experienced by older workers may result in their employment status 
being more fluid than those of prime-age workers. Successful SCSEP programs empower participants to achieve 
a livable wage in a fulfilling job that is suited to their talents, abilities, and expectations.  
Through skills training, work experience, and access to supportive services, Goodwill SCSEP serves as a bridge for 
program participants to enter or reenter the workforce. Goodwill SCSEP has developed strong relationships with 
employer partners, including host agencies, to facilitate job placements for participants—often in rural 
communities where older workers may experience limited job prospects.  
Goodwill SCSEP employer partners are able to access an underutilized segment of the workforce to fill a wide 
range of positions with the knowledge that SCSEP participants have the foundational skills and on-the-job 
experience they need for success. Goodwill SCSEP utilizes surveys to report on employer satisfaction with the 
program, and the qualitative elements of these surveys provide an additional depth of insight that helps to 
inform program design and delivery. We urge the Department to retain the current definition and practices for 
measuring effectiveness of SCSEP programs in serving employers. 
Recommendations: 
• 
Clarify intentions to engage in rulemaking that would seek to change the definition of the 
performance indicator of effectiveness in serving employers as it applies to SCSEP. 
• 
Ensure SCSEP grantees and stakeholders can provide feedback and share concerns about any 
proposed changes in performance accountability.   
• 
Retain the current definition and practices for assessing effectiveness of SCSEP programs in serving 
employers. 
Goodwill is working to strengthen America’s workforce by helping people with barriers to employment, 
including older workers and people involved in the justice system, obtain the skills, competencies, and 
credentials needed to pursue high-quality careers in in-demand fields. Thank you for your thoughtful 

consideration of these recommendations, and we hope you will continue to engage Goodwill as a resource in 
this important work. Please contact GII’s Government Relations Senior Specialist Mitch Coppes at (240) 333-
5394 or mitch.coppes@goodwill.org with any questions you may have.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Laura Walling, Esq. 
Vice President of Government Affairs

SUBJECT: Public Comment to NPRM Re: Employer Effectiveness Measures 
 
The Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training appreciates the opportunity to comment on 
the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning TEGL 10-16, Change 2 - Performance 
Accountability Guidance for Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Core 
Programs – concerning Effectiveness in Serving Employers (ESE) indicators under WIOA. The 
Department acknowledges the merit of measuring employer effectiveness in a dual-customer 
WIOA system and further acknowledges how difficult it is to identify an employer effectiveness 
measure that is reliable, representative, and easy to administer. Rhode Island tracked all three 
pilot measures during the trial performance period. We observed that each measure had their 
own strengths and weaknesses. We will address these, as well as our observations and concerns 
with selecting Retention with the Same Employer as the single ESE indicator, below: 
 
• Employer penetration is useful as a measure of ‘brand awareness’ but is more an 
indicator of quantity, not quality/satisfaction. It’s also a lagging/secondary indicator in 
that if we are performing well for employers and they are ‘satisfied’ with our services; 
then our penetration rate should, in theory, increase. 
• Repeat business customer is a bit more useful as measure but lacks context based on the 
industry and employer. In our experience, repeat business customers in WIOA are not 
that uncommon, but they may be more attracted to the financial benefit of programs like 
OJTs or IWT than satisfied with a particular outcome or service.     
• Of all proposed/current or theoretical measures, Retention with Same Employer is the 
easiest for Rhode Island to administer and the most consistent to apply across WIOA 
programs. 
• Retention also better indicates some level of employer satisfaction, or at least the absence 
of dissatisfaction, with the placement.  
• However, retention does not speak to acuity of placement (for example; how difficult the 
position was to fill, how in-demand the position is, whether the role was seasonal specific 
and not intended to maintain retention, rarity of skill set, time to hire, etc.). 
• Retention may not be the desired outcome for the job seeker, especially if the placement 
is in a lower wage position, nor does retention reflect whether the employee is required to 
work at more than one employer to maintain a living wage.  
• Retention does not currently speak to what business service, if any, the employer 
received.  
• Retention combined with some measure of acuity (skill/education level of the position, 
time to placement, etc.) and the ability to filter for those employers who received a 
business service, would improve the measure.   
Again, the Department appreciates the opportunity to comment on the NPRM and would be 
happy to provide additional information and comment upon request.
